After traveling across time in The Terminator and to the outer reaches of deep space in Aliens, they have now journeyed into the Cayman Trough - one of the deepest and most impenetrable chasms on earth - for The Abyss. Set in an underwater oil drilling habitat located seventeen hundred feet beneath the ocean surface, the film begins with the search for a downed nuclear submarine and evolves into an aquatic odyssey of cosmic consequence. Forty percent of the production was shot in the largest fresh water filming tank in the world - a specially converted reactor containment building located at an uncommissioned nuclear power plant. Nine visual effects units were engaged to produce literally hundreds of shots covering the gamut of cinematic illusions from computer generated imagery and motion control to animatronic puppets and radio control vehicles to matte paintings and underwater miniatures to rear projection and bluescreen traveling mattes. Virtually no effects technique was left untapped. A trio of distinguished effects supervisors - John Bruno and Hoyt Yeatman and Dennis Muren - oversaw the activities of in-house units and teams from Dream Quest Images and Industrial Light and Magic. Ancillary units were headed by Cameron veterans Robert and Dennis Skotak and Gene Warren of Fantasy II. Though photographed thousands of miles apart - in situations both wet and dry and by artists of diverse talents and experience - the effects blended together seamlessly with the main unit photography and with one another. The end result is an unprecedented and uncompromising accomplishment - an epic film of wonder and imagination propelled by the singular vision and relentless drive of a master filmmaker just hitting his stride. Something is out there - something of indeterminate origin closing on the ballistic missile carrier at nautical speeds far in excess of anything known to man. The unseen signal source overtakes the warship with ease and deftly alters course to avoid it. Too late. Caught in a turbulent shockwave, the submarine hammers into a rocky canyon wall. Its pressure hull ruptures on impact and within moments the waterlogged vessel slides crumbling into the Cayman Trough - one of the deepest and most impenetrable chasms on earth. With no hope for survivors, priority one for the Navy is to locate the billion dollar wreckage and sanitize its top secret documents and weaponry. A gathering storm threatens to make the area untenable for surface support ships. Only one option remains. Twenty miles away on the ocean bottom lies Deepcore II - a prototype oil drilling platform with a crew of ten and a full complement of underwater probes and submersible vehicles. With approval from Benthic Petroleum - overseer of the Deepcore project - the Navy dispatches a SEAL team to the drilling rig with orders that all on-site personnel and resources are to be commandeered for the recovery operation. For writer-director James Cameron, The Abyss was a natural outgrowth of his passion for scuba diving. "The Jacques Cousteau series was airing when I was in high school and I loved all of that stuff and really wanted to learn how to dive. But my attraction to it was always visual - I never associated it with the sensation of what it would be like to immerse yourself totally in water and breathe off a breathing system. That turned out to be very strange. I was dive certified at the age of seventeen and since then have always wanted to do something that incorporated film and diving - I wanted to do the definitive diving movie, But what do you do? Show the beauties of the coral reef or the perils of killer sharks? Those films have already been done. What I wanted was to go into the realm that had always excited me the most because of its extremes and its absoluteness - I wanted to go deep into the ocean." Shortly after Aliens went into release, Cameron began formulating characters and situations for a deep-sea thriller. With a comprehensive treatment in hand - and together with his producer and then-wife Gale Anne Hurd - he presented the project to Twentieth Century Fox and secured from the studio a tentative commitment to back the independent feature conditional upon the submission of a finished script and a reasonable budget. Using a short story he had written in high school as a point of departure, Cameron proceeded to develop a dramatic screenplay set principally in a vast subaquatic habitat seventeen hundred feet below the surface of the ocean. "Only one essential element was retained from my original short story. In high school, I participated in a weekly science seminar where different speakers were brought in to talk about everything from childbirth to the latest advances in physics. One of those speakers happened to be a commercial diver who had participated in an experiment in which he had breathed with a liquid in both lungs for something like forty-five minutes. That really blew my mind. Here was a guy who had used his lungs as a gill mechanism. From that seminar came the idea for a story I wrote about some scientists in a research installation on a cliff overlooking the Cayman Trough. Using liquid breathing suits, they begin making forays into the deepest depths of the ocean - but no one who goes down the cliff comes back again." Although fluid breathing would play an essential role in The Abyss, that concept and the title were the only elements retained from the original short story, "When I began working on The Abyss, I took the kernel of that one idea and incorporated it into the script. But the whole research thing was definitely out. Audiences don't give a rat's ass about scientists anymore. My characters are blue collar workers who just happen to get involved in a big military operation to try and find out what happened to this nuclear submarine - and in the process, they discover something truly extraordinary." To prepare his audience for the truly extraordinary, Cameron had to establish a solid groundwork for the artificial reality of his underwater habitat. 'The film has two layers of fantasy, One is the fantasy that five or ten years from now, the physical environment of this movie will exist. A wholly submersible drilling platform does not exist today. The second layer of fantasy is what happens when the people working on this drilling platform come upon something much more fantastic than their daily lives. In order to best sell that idea to an audience, I decided to take the low-grade fantasy of this near-future submersible drilling station and make it a fraudulent reality of today. The dialogue is perfectly contemporary: the clothing is perfectly contemporary: the facility is modeled room for room on existing offshore semi-submersible drilling platforms. Very deliberately I took advantage of the fact that we live in a time when technological advances are so rapid on so many fronts that the average person has no real idea what is possible today and what is not. We live in a science fiction world." Among the earliest principals to become involved in the project was effects supervisor John Bruno. An Oscar nominee for his work on Ghostbusters and Poltergeist II, Bruno had served terms at Industrial Light and Magic and Boss Film Corporation and had recently stepped out of effects to develop and direct Lone Wolfe and Cub- a Japanese samurai film transposed to the American West. "Jim and I had met briefly at a screening of Aliens and then again at an effects seminar in Japan," said Bruno. "We kept in touch after that -and when The Abyss came along, Jim talked to me about possibly visualizing some of the images and helping him attract the right people to the project. He knew that it was going to be a film on a higher level than he had done before - and since I knew most of the key players, he thought I might make a good gobetween to help him place the project at one of the major effects companies." With his own project stalled in a financial morass, Bruno was persuaded by Cameron to stay on through

the storyboarding phase. "I hired Phill Norwood to work with me on the boards and between us we did them all. Meanwhile, Jim was trying to convince me to be effects supervisor. I was hesitant to commit fully; but since my own project was still in limbo, I agreed to help him hire an effects company and place all the shots." Before that could be done, the storyboards had to be logged into a computer and then put into book form so they could be sent around to all of the major effects houses for bids. "The most difficult part of the process was getting the effects budget down somewhere within this stratosphere. When Jim and I first began talking about it, I looked at everything he wanted to do and off the top of my head came up with a figure in the $8 million range. And he said, 'Nah, no way. Well, the first round of bids came back almost double that." "The lowest bid was $13 million and the highest was $16 million," Cameron shuddered. "I suspect my low bid was higher than any other effects bid in history. But that was it - the film was not going to get made. Fox had bought themselves a script and we had spent some money on storyboards and such - but there was no way anyone was going to make this movie. After I recovered from shock, I decided to try another approach and began by cutting out eighty of the original two hundred and sixty effects shots. Then I divided the remaining shots up by technique. There would be model shots done wet-for-wet; there would be model shots done dry-for-wet in smoke; there would be surface miniatures and matte paintings and computer generated imagery. In all - seven distinct groupings. Two of them - the wet-for-wet shots and the surface model shots - I decided we would do ourselves. Any of the companies we were dealing with would have to set up special units to do those, so it made sense not to pay someone else's overhead when we could just as well do them ourselves as part of the normal production. The remaining five we put out for bid. A company could bid on more than one unit, but I withheld the right to award them separately if I chose to. That really opened things up. It also took the fear factor out of doing the whole show. No matter how hard the shots were, a small number of them would be manageable over a nine-or ten-month period. It was probably the most intensely competitive effects bidding ever - and we started getting back some good numbers." When the process was completed, Dream Quest Images and Industrial Light and Magic emerged as the principal players. The Abyss was again on the production docket. Cameron and Hurd - both expert divers - gave no thought to filming The Abyss anywhere but in a water environment. There would be no smoked stages with actors in weighted suits. Only the real thing was acceptable. But with forty percent of the scripted action taking place underwater, it was certain to be the most elaborate and difficult film of its type ever mounted. For a picture of such magnitude, one person was considered essential and Cameron moved quickly to secure a commitment from him. In a career spanning three decades, underwater cinematographer Al Giddings had worked on dozens of features CINEFEX 39 • 7 MONTANA 1-74

ranging from The Deep to Never Say Never Again. No one else in the business could remotely approach his level of expertise. Once on board, the veteran diver was instrumental in providing early counsel and in helping to evaluate possible shooting sites. "The ocean was never an option," stated Cameron. "If I ever considered it for a second, it was out of total desperation. On Piranha II- my unmentionable movie - I had actually tried doing that. We put a set underwater one afternoon - and when we came back the next day to shoot we found that it had been destroyed overnight by a tidal surge that was practically imperceptible. So I knew that the ocean fights you every step of the way. We had to find a tank." Not just any tank would suffice. A bigtank was needed - big enough to sustain not only divers and submersible vehicles, but also a sizable portion of the Deepcore drilling platform at full scale. "We checked out every tank facility worldwide," said Gale Anne Hurd, "and quickly discovered that there was really nothing suitable for a film of this size and scope. Most of them were simply too small - but even the ones that were large enough had drawbacks. Many of them were just surface tanks and not designed for underwater photography. So the chances of getting an image on film with any sort of clarity were minimal. The saltwater tank in Malta - which is the largest in the world - has been used for underwater work on occasion, but it is unfiltered and unheated. Water temperature was a major concern. Even in relatively warm water - around seventy-two degrees - hypothermia would have kept us from working underwater for the twelve hours a day we knew would be necessary. We needed water that was about eighty-five degrees. At one point we thought the old Marineland facility just south of Los Angeles might be an option. It had been closed for several years and was going to be developed into a residential area. We would have had to change our approach a bit because the tanks there were not as deep as we would have liked - but there were facilities for heating and filtering water and there was a large glass window for observation. But for insurance reasons or whatever, the owners decided not to make it available to us." Building a suitable tank from scratch was not an option; but it occurred to the filmmakers that if some preexisting vessel large enough and strong enough were located, it might be feasible to retrofit it with pumps and filters and fill it with water. A broadened search pattern eventually led them to the uncompleted Cherokee Nuclear Power Plant near the small town of Gaffney in rural South Carolina. With $700 million expended on the complex, Duke Power Company had abruptly halted construction and abandoned the site in 1983, leaving behind a cluster of half-finished concrete structures and a few prefabricated warehouses. Show business entrepreneur Earl Owensby - a freewheeling actor-producer with a reputation for making low-budget drive-in fodder - had subsequently purchased the facility for $3 million and was touting it as a full-service film studio. Cameron was drawn to the place even before he saw it. "I knew that nuclear power stations have large water reservoirs and that the government sets very high specs for their construction. So I thought it possible that there might be some buildings there that could be used as tanks even if they were designed for something altogether different. I spoke with Earl and he said: 'Come on down, son. Have I got a tank for youl So Al Giddings and I went down there and Earl showed us his tank - and it was heart-wrenching because all it was was the foundation of the turbine pit. It was full of bull rushes and had rebars sticking up all over and I couldn't even see how deep it was because it was partially flooded. It certainly would not have worked for what I had in mind. It was pouring rain that day and I looked through the skeletal structure of the turbine building and beyond it was this big concrete cylinder sticking up out of the ground. I asked Earl what it was and he said, That's going to be my two-thousand-seat amphitheater.' And I said, 'Okay, let's take a look at it.' So we drove over there and we're looking at it from the outside, and I said, 'How do you get in?' And he said: 'You caint. The way you go in is flooded.' So I walked all the way around it and, sure enough, there was no way into this thing. But standing next to it was a giant gantry crane -a hundred and seventy-five feet tall - so I decided to climb up to the top and take a look. Not to be outdone, Al Giddings put his Nikon strap in his mouth and climbed up after me. So there we were - out on this boom swaying around in the wind and the rain - and below us was this enormous concave dish. It looked like the Coliseum in Rome." Jim Cameron had found his tank. The Owensby amphitheater was in fact the unfinished containment building designed to house the power plant's nuclear reactor. Two hundred feet in diameter and fifty-five feet in depth, the above-ground structure would eventually house instead a gigantic movie set and some seven-and-a-half million gallons of water. At first, however, the inherent obstacles seemed almost insurmountable. "We began to take the power plant seriously," said Hurd, "when Earl indicated that he would be willing to convert the containment building and the turbine pit into serviceable filming tanks. It was going to be no small undertaking. The containment building had huge gaps in the concrete that would have to be filled before it could even begin to hold water. Both structures were loaded with rebar that would have to removed. And, of course, there would have to be pumping systems and filtration equipment and heaters installed. We sent in a number of engineering consultants, and when they reported that the containment building could be converted - and theoretically converted in time - we decided to go forward." A contract was entered into by both parties. In exchange for payments totalling $2.25 million from the production company, Earl Owensby would transform his concrete structures into gigantic water tanks suitable for set construction and filming. He would also renovate other buildings into production offices and dressing rooms and would make the studio available to the company from the time construction began through the end of principal photography in December 1988. Though an accomplished artist in his own right, Cameron had recognized early on the need for additional input and inspiration in the design of his underwater habitat and its attendant vehicles. Having established a solid rapport with Ron Cobb on Aliens, it was not surprising that he should turn once again to the veteran technologist when it came time to formalize the visual elements of The Abyss. Cobb was drawn at once to the Deepcore habitat which was clearly the visual centerpiece of the film. "My primary role was to come out of the blue with a basic concept of what the thing might look like - even Jim had no real sense of it early on. It seemed to me that a modular configuration would make a lot of sense - with an adjustable framework so that one module could be lifted out and replaced with another if need be. Also the entire habitat could be made larger or smaller as its function expanded or diminished. Jim felt that it ought to have a vertical look, so I began gravitating toward the idea of using vertical cylinders - each with three decks - positioned into trimodule configurations within a giant spaceframe. There were endless variations as to how we could arrange these trimodules - it was like using a big tinker toy set. Coming up with something logical was the main challenge - that and giving it a sense of design evolution. Almost everything that surrounds us - from automobiles to jetliners to television sets - has been been refined and thought through for years and years. So the real task in designing any future technology is to give the impression that it has gone through that same kind The final Deepcore design consisted of two trimodules and two bimodules clustered together and interconnected with a network of tubular passageways. In true scale the complex would have covered more than twenty thousand square feet of the ocean floor - dwarfing to insignificance the largest undersea habitat in actual employment, yet a full fifty percent smaller "Deepcore went through a lot of than originally conceived. revisions," Cobb continued. "The initial grand concept was that it would be a virtual city underwater and that we would build just a small part of it in the tank and then pick up the slack with a miniature. But as we got into it, Jim wanted to put more and more of it into the water and so we began to shrink the whole thing down - refining it and refining it and tucking more and more of it into the tank." Though connected to a surface vessel via an umbilical tether, the complex itself was capable of independent movement from one drilling site to the next. "Around the perimeter of the spaceframe were vertical thrusters designed to lift Deepcore off the bottom and keep it level. Then there were longitudinal thrusters - two above and two below to bracket the center of gravity - that would kick in and push the whole thing through the water. In that way it could fly slowly over the bottom to a new drilling location and then settle down on hydraulic skids simply by shutting off its longitudinal thrusters. I spent a lot of time designing an undersea automated derrick that could pick up drill pipes and then feed them into a traveling block. In an early version of the script there was going to be a sequence where the oil well was disengaged and the derrick folded down onto Deepcore as preparations got underway for it to move. So the derrick was all mechanized to pivot into place - but the sequence was subsequently cut and the derrick with its tilting mechanisms is now simply texture on the model." Responsibility for translating the Deepcore concepts into three-dimensional reality fell to production designer Leslie Dilley - an Oscar winner for art direction on Star Wars and Raiders lost are of the Lost Ark who had worked previously with Ron Cobb designs on Alien. Before substantive work could commence on the underwater drilling complex, Earl Owensby and his contractors had to render the containment building capable of holding more than twenty-five thousand tons of water. "Everyone felt confident that the structure would hold the water," said Dilley, "because it was made of concrete that was three feet thick in most places. But it was not watertight by any means. There were a lot of holes in it that would have allowed water to flow out and through a pipe system to the turbine pit - which was to be our other tank. All those had to be filled. Since the construction had never been completed, there were huge gaps in the walls and in the actual bowl itself. Those had to be filled in also - which was difficult because it was all splayed on a curve. After the major holes were treated, the entire tank had to be surfaced with gunite and sealers." With construction underway at the Owensby facility, Cameron was back in Los Angeles orchestrating the preproduction effort. Casting the film would encompass far more than the customary evaluation of acting credentials and interpersonal chemistry. "We made it clear from the start that the actors in this picture were going to be diving a lot and that anyone who had serious qualms about that had better not get involved. I deliberately tried to scare them so that anyone who was claustrophobic or afraid of the water would admit it before we went through screen testing and contracts and all that." Resisting studio pressure to cast bankable boxoffice stars, Cameron selected Ed Harris for the role of Deepcore rig foreman Bud Brigman and Mary Elizabeth Mastrantonio as his project director and estranged wife Lindsey. Filling out the leads was Cameron perennial Michael Biehn as the SEAL team leader Lieutenant Coffey, Since most of the actors had no diving experience, all were flown to Grand Cayman for a week of intensive training. Certified on mouth regulators and masks, they would later need to learn helmet diving before the start of underwater shooting. In researching commercial diving helmets, Cameron had found that visibility was a universal limiting factor. Most existing units had either a single large faceplate or a smaller one augmented with lateral and overhead viewing ports. In either case, visibility was less than optimal - looking out or looking in. If he was going to have his actors performing underwater, Cameron wanted to make certain that their vision was largely

unimpaired. Equally important, he had to be sure that his principal cast members were recognizable on camera. Western Space and Marine vice president Robert Kirby - codesigner of two industry standard helmets - was contacted regarding the problem and promptly committed his Santa Barbara firm to the construction of ten functional helmet prototypes if the production company could come up with a workable design. Ron Cobb set to the task. "It occurred to me that the simplest approach to increasing visibility would be to take a plexiglass 'plus sign' and bend the tabs back to produce kind of a wraparound window with all flat surfaces. There would be a little band of distortion right at the bend, but it really opened up the sight lines. From there it was a matter of just fitting it to the human face and working out where the regulator would go and allowing for head clearance and all that stuff. Jim was also involved a lot. When we got it just the way we wanted, I drew it up very carefully and we sent it off to Western Space Within a month of receiving the helmet drawings, Robert Kirby was able to produce a fully realized engineering concept that successfully merged both aesthetic desires and functional requisites. Another six months would be needed to construct the working prototypes. Essential machine elements were fabricated in-house by Troy Kirby while fiberglass sections were produced by Larry Smith. Visibility was a prime concern. The wraparound faceplate - formed from a polycarbonate resin used in shatterproof windows - served the divers well but did not always render their faces readily identifiable. "To make certain that the actors could be seen," said Troy Kirby, "one of the things we had to do was provide some illumination within the helmet. When we first discussed the problem with Jim Cameron, we suggested simply putting some lights inside. He said: 'God, nol What practical reason could there be to have lights on the inside of a helmet?' So the trick became how to throw some light onto the actors without making it look obvious. Since an external working light was already part of the helmet design, we decided to take that existing lamp and incorporate into it a fifty-fifty beamsplitter that directed some of the illumination down through a piece of diffused glass and out over the faceplate. The result was subtle and variable and very effective." With eight weeks of underwater shooting before him, Cameron was adamant that the helmets be equipped with an effective communication system that would enable him to record live dialogue and direct underwater as he would anywhere else. No such system existed. "Most underwater cameramen come from documentary backgrounds and so they do not think in terms of stage production or normal production parameters. The standard routine is to have a cue light on the camera. The director points to the actor and then points to the cue light and that means the actor is supposed to start acting. That has been the state of the art in underwater filming. Underwater diver address systems have been used - where sound is blasted out into the water through speakers so everyone can hear - but usually in those situations the director is topside watching through a video monitor and talking down below. That was equally unacceptable to me. I had to be there in the water and Thad to be able to speak directly to my cast and crew." Western Space and Marine president Scott Millard and engineer Robin Gauss complied by equipping each helmet with earphones and an aircraft quality microphone that not only allowed Cameron to give verbal directions to his cast and crew, but also enabled spoken dialogue to be recorded directly onto tape - a first in underwater filmmaking. Even at a hefty twenty-six pounds - rendered neutrally buoyant in water - the helmets were considerably lighter than anything else on the commercial market. Each unit was equipped with a latch mechanism that attached to a fitting in a flexible rubber collar worn by the diver. Because of this collar, the helmet could be used even without a wet suit - an option favored by Cameron who often directed underwater wearing only swim trunks and a Hawaiian shirt. Clearly the most userfriendly feature of the helmet was its 'on demand' breathing regulator - a decided upgrade over mouthpiece regulators currently standard in commercial diving helmets. "When the diver needs to breathe," said Kirby, "a servo-driven regulator on the right side of his helmet senses it and brings in air automatically. The air comes up and out of some sinus-like cavities on the inside of the helmet and the diver is able to breathe quite normally. It is very comfortable and nonclaustrophobic. With every breath, the system also washes CO, out of the helmet and clears the faceplate - like an instant defroster." Although true commercial divers invariably work with an umbilical lifeline that provides a constant source of air from the surface, Cameron wanted his divers to be untethered - thus requiring a modified scuba approach. For the air supply, hydraulic engineer Brian Macy modified a stock triple backpack - a unit originally designed for Jacques Cousteau. Though the tank capacity was ninety cubic feet of air - enough to support a diver for slightly more than an hour - the filmmakers still had a dilemma. With a dozen or more people underwater at all times, someone would invariably be needing to surface for air. To circumvent this disruption, Western Space and Marine developed an underwater refilling station that would enable the divers' tanks to be recharged quickly without surfacing. In his script, Cameron had provided Deepcore with a small complement of manned submersibles to aid crew members in underwater maintenance and exploration. Cab One and Cab Three were simple transport and observation vehicles much like actual research submersibles currently in use. Flatbed was a larger and more fancifully conceived extrapolation designed specifically to support underwater drilling operations. "We are a commercial diving service," explained project manager James English, "which means essentially that we will do just about anything underwater. Because we have this arsenal of equipment and expertise - and because this movie involved so much underwater work - we were approached by the production company to be their diving experts and also to provide them with the submersibles that they needed." Cameron was most interested in Can-Dive's custom-built Deep Rover submersible which was capable of operating effectively in waters up to three thousand feet deep. With some addon modifications to alter its squatty profile, he felt that the oneperson sub - with its spherical acrylic hull and two large manipulator arms - would be ideal for the Flatbed vehicle he had envisioned in his script. Unfortunately, the one-of-a-kind unit was already committed to a long-term scientific project. Since nothing else in the inventory was considered appropriate, the only workable solution was to build something new from scratch. Unfettered by the necessity to retrofit an existing vehicle, Ron Cobb was able to approach the Flatbed design with his usual passion for functional efficiency. "Jim was insistent on using real waves for the advancing and receding shots - and I pretty much agreed with him, although we were ready to back up and try something else if that did not work. We looked around at other options - Fiji and Chile and Capetown - but the problem with those places is that they have no satellite system to predict when the big waves are going to come. Boom! - we're on the beach at Santa Monica. Now all of a sudden the audience is forced to be a character. The only way for me to do a film and not get totally involved in the effects is to make a film that has no effects - but the relationship is definitely a love-hate affair. I hate effects because I know they are an Achilles heel - a weak link in the process where your film can fall down badly and lose its sense of reality. On the other hand, effects can also be the place where you blow people away. There are a lot of effects in The Abyss - most of them very good. But the most powerful moments - the moments I am certain will blow people away in this film - have no effects at all.
